The increase in the global adoption of technologies such as solar, wind, and batteries has further spiked the demand for shipping, and the limited U.S. share (around 1%) of the world’s shipbuilding industry puts the United States at a strategic disadvantage, subtly boosting China’s influence at a grand strategy level (Brooks 2025). Advocating for support to the U.S. shipbuilding industry could help address this risk. 4.1.2 Access To Foreign Energy Grids China’s leadership in advanced energy development and manufacturing has enabled it to access foreign energy grids by supplying low-cost equipment and infrastructure. This creates potential cyber and influence risks for DOW operations that rely on local power systems while also providing a publicly accepted justification for Chinese presence near U.S. activities that may conceal covert intentions. Since 2013, Chinese companies have completed 369 overseas power projects through the Belt and Road Initiative, totaling 156 GW of capacity (Thomton et al. 2025). The State Grid Corporation of China has secured stakes in regional power grids, such as 40% ownership of the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (Morales, Jerome, and Lopez 2025). At DOW’s overseas military bases across 55 countries and territories (Nicastro and Tilghman 2024), the risks associated with relying on civilian infrastructure are compounded by limited U.S. authority and control over energy technology components and infrastructure. Third-party providers could introduce vulnerabilities, particularly in regions where foreign influence can extend to critical military infrastructure. As industry leaders and low-cost bidders, Chinese firms are increasingly winning solar energy contracts across Pacific Island nations (Xinhua 2024). In Europe, Chinese firms are likely to gain greater access to Germany’s power grid if proposed legislation to improve solar energy integration is passed, creating new opportunities for Chinese solar inverter manufacturers (Wehrmann 2025). Moreover, many wind turbines in Germany use Chinese-made parts, raising concerns about potential foreign influence on this technology (Wehrmann 2025). This pervasive access for monitoring, control, and software management further exacerbates the cyber risk arising from electrification because energy assets, whether manufactured domestically or in friendly nations, pose a cyber risk if they contain embedded electronics sourced from potential adversaries or require maintenance directly from original equipment manufacturers. DOW microgrids with high cybersecurity standards, point-of-need generation, and inside-the-fence backup power would help mitigate this risk. 4.1.3 Access Near DOW Facilities and Operations Having successfully taken the commercial lead in advanced energy technology manufacturing and development, China-based companies are often a top choice of U.S. firms and communities looking to develop advanced energy inputs or infrastructure, allowing China to expand its presence in U.S. territory, possibly near DOW facilities or operations, and creating the potential for Chinese surveillance.
